stories.title: Synopsys and A*STAR team up on chiplet packaging study
stories.summary: The deal gives Singapore chip firms early access to simulation tools aimed at cutting packaging risk and speeding AI and HPC development.
stories.content:
Mon, 21st Sep 2026 (Yesterday)
Synopsys and Singapore's Agency for Science, Technology and Research have signed a memorandum of understanding on semiconductor packaging and simulation technologies.

The agreement focuses on advanced packaging and chiplet-based architectures through A*STAR's Institute of Microelectronics.

The collaboration will run through the A*STAR IME-Ansys Joint Innovation Consortium for Semiconductor Excellence, or JICSE. The consortium brings together A*STAR's Institute of Microelectronics and Ansys, now part of Synopsys, as a platform for joint research and development in advanced system-in-package technologies.

At its core is a push to use digital modelling and analysis earlier in semiconductor development. As packages grow more complex, chipmakers and electronics companies are trying to identify design, reliability and performance issues before building physical prototypes, with the aim of reducing development time and manufacturing risk.

That shift is making packaging a more strategic part of the semiconductor supply chain. While chip design has long drawn most of the industry's attention, advanced packaging is becoming more important as companies seek to improve computing performance, manage power and integrate multiple functions into smaller systems.

Chiplet-based designs are part of that shift. Instead of building all functions onto a single large chip, manufacturers can combine several smaller dies in one package. The method is increasingly used in artificial intelligence and high-performance computing systems, where performance, yield and cost all matter.

### Consortium focus

JICSE's initial phase will focus on mechanical design, modelling and analysis. Areas of work include package and wafer warpage, thermo-mechanical stress, solder joint reliability and moisture-induced failures in multi-chiplet architectures.

These issues are central to whether advanced semiconductor products can be manufactured at scale. Warpage can affect assembly and alignment, thermal stress can shorten product life, and solder joint failures remain a common reliability concern as packages become denser and more complex.

Moreover, the consortium will explore research projects with academic institutions and offer technical training programmes and seminars for industry participants. A*STAR IME will lead consortium-based research and development, drawing on its expertise in advanced packaging and applied research.

Synopsys will support adoption of simulation-led design methods by providing trial licences for its Ansys simulation software to A*STAR IME and up to 10 consortium member companies. The arrangement suggests the partners want to broaden access to modelling tools among local companies, not just large multinational groups with established in-house simulation resources.

### Singapore role

The deal also reflects Singapore's effort to strengthen its position in semiconductors beyond fabrication and assembly. The city-state has long hosted manufacturing and test operations for global chip groups, but policymakers and public research bodies have increasingly sought to deepen local expertise in higher-value areas including design, packaging and process development.

A*STAR has played a central role in that strategy by linking public research institutes with industry projects. Its Institute of Microelectronics has been involved in packaging, sensors and materials research, often working with commercial partners on technologies that can move into production settings.

For Synopsys, the agreement offers access to a research and industry network focused on packaging challenges at a time when design software groups are trying to expand beyond traditional electronic design automation. Simulation tools used for thermal, structural and reliability analysis are becoming more relevant as semiconductor and systems engineering increasingly overlap.

Terence Gan, Executive Director, A*STAR IME, set out the institute's view of the partnership.

"Advanced packaging is fast becoming a critical differentiator in global semiconductor innovation, particularly as systems grow more complex and AI-driven. Through this collaboration with Synopsys, A*STAR IME is combining our R&D expertise with Synopsys' line of Ansys simulation technologies to co-develop next-generation semiconductor packaging and simulation technologies. This enables companies to innovate with greater speed and confidence, and reinforces Singapore's position as a leading hub for semiconductor innovation," Gan said.

His comments implicate a broader industry trend in which packaging is no longer treated solely as a back-end manufacturing task. Instead, it is becoming a design consideration from the earliest development stages, particularly for processors and systems aimed at artificial intelligence workloads.

Synopsys also framed the work as part of a wider move towards system-level design and modelling.

"The future of semiconductor innovation is going to be increasingly defined by how effectively complex systems are designed and integrated. Through this collaboration with A*STAR IME and the launch of JICSE, Synopsys is committed to empowering an industry-wide shift toward simulation-led, system-driven design. This collaboration aims to back local companies in Singapore for tackling key challenges in reliability, performance, and scalability - while also fast-tracking the time-to-market for next-generation AI and HPC technologies," said Moon.

The agreement leaves open how many companies will ultimately join the consortium, but the initial software access for up to 10 members gives the initiative an early framework as Singapore seeks to build deeper semiconductor expertise in advanced packaging.

stories.title: AirTrunk said to seek US$1.6 billion loan for Singapore REIT listing
stories.summary: Blackstone-backed AirTrunk has approached banks for a US$1.6 billion loan spanning tranches of three to seven years, to fund a planned Singapore REIT listing of its assets, Bloomberg reports. The financing would support one of the largest data centre REITs in Asia.
stories.why_it_matters: A Singapore REIT listing would give AirTrunk a recurring capital recycling vehicle and APAC investors a liquid way into hyperscale data centre income. The loan structure suggests banks remain willing to underwrite large digital-infrastructure exposure, even as some lenders grow cautious on the sector.
stories.content:
Blackstone-backed data center operator AirTrunk, is seeking US$1.6 billion loan to finance an upcoming proposed public listing of a real estate investment trust (REIT) in Singapore, according to Bloomberg recently citing people familiar with the matter.

AirTrunk is said to have sent requests to banks seeking several tranches of loan ranging between three and seven years in Singapore dollars and yen. The loan, to be raised by the REIT, will most likely be used to acquire assets from AirTrunk and refinance existing debt, the people added. The IPO will allow AirTrunk to raise capital from a wider pool of investors.

When asked, representatives from both AirTrunk and Blackstone declined to comment.

In June, __w.media__ reported that AirTrunk was about to file confidentially for a REIT IPO in Singapore, according to people familiar with the matter.

Data center loans in the region have hit almost US$ 29 billion since the beginning of 2025, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Banks are getting more selective as they are nearing their sector limits.

stories.title: Micron demonstrates 512GB DDR5 module for next-gen AI servers
stories.summary: Micron has shown what it calls the world's first 512GB DDR5 memory module, aimed at next-generation server platforms, with volume production expected in the second half of 2027. The module promises higher memory density and better power efficiency for AI and analytics workloads.
stories.why_it_matters: Doubling per-module capacity lets AI server builders pack more memory per rack, easing one of the biggest bottlenecks in large-model training and inference. Cloud providers planning 2027 hardware refreshes can now design around denser configurations, with knock-on effects for data centre power and space planning.
stories.content:
Micron Technology Inc. has successfully demonstrated the world's first 512GB DDR5 module on multiple server platforms, marking a significant advancement in high-capacity server memory. This development provides enterprise data center and cloud customers with a clear path to support increasingly demanding artificial intelligence (AI), analytics, in-memory database, and simulation-heavy workloads with enhanced efficiency. The module is expected to reach volume production in the second half of 2027.The new ultra-dense module, which will deliver speeds up to 9,200 MT/s, leverages Micron’s advanced vertical interconnect packaging innovations. This technology vertically stacks DRAM dies interconnected by through-silicon vias (TSVs), maximising density within individual DRAM packages while maintaining the performance required by modern data center architectures. A single 24-slot dual-socket server can now enable up to 12 terabytes (TB) of DDR5 DRAM, significantly expanding memory capabilities within existing server footprints.Raj Narasimhan, Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Cloud Memory Business Unit at Micron, highlighted that the 512GB RDIMM enables multi-terabyte servers, supporting larger AI and database workloads, greater virtualization density, and improved power efficiency. This allows customers to keep larger datasets closer to compute engines, reducing reliance on slower storage tiers and minimising costly data movement.Leading semiconductor enablers, AMD and Intel, are actively collaborating with Micron to validate the 512GB DDR5 RDIMM across next-generation server platforms. This close engineering partnership aims to ensure broad compatibility and a smooth path to deployment for data center operators and cloud infrastructure teams. Amit Goel, Corporate Vice President, Compute and Enterprise AI Platform Solutions Engineering at AMD, noted that this collaboration brings compute and memory innovation together to help customers realise the full value of AMD-powered platforms for balanced, high-performance infrastructure. Similarly, Karin Eibschitz Segal, General Manager of Platform and System Engineering in Intel’s Data Center Group, emphasised that Intel is working closely with Micron to enable future server platforms designed for the growing demands of next-generation data center workloads.The rapid proliferation of large language models (LLMs), agentic AI, real-time inference, and high-core-count CPU workloads is driving the demand for greater server memory capacity, higher bandwidth, and improved power efficiency. Micron's 512GB RDIMMs directly address these requirements. The new module reduces operating power by more than 60 per cent compared with four 128GB RDIMMs. For memory-bound workloads such as Spark Support Vector Machines (SVM)-based data analytics, these RDIMMs can deliver up to 1.4 times higher performance compared to 256GB DDR5 configurations. Additionally, the 512GB module provides significant advantages for memory-intensive databases and caching platforms like RocksDB and Redis, improving throughput, increasing concurrency, and scaling datasets more efficiently.Darrin Alves, CIO for Infrastructure Platforms at JPMorganChase, commented that higher-capacity memory technologies like Micron’s 512GB RDIMMs will help enterprises support larger in-memory workloads, improve resource utilisation, and enhance the flexibility needed to scale modern computing environments.Data center operators, cloud infrastructure teams, enterprise infrastructure leaders, and AI infrastructure stakeholders should monitor Micron's 512GB DDR5 RDIMM development for future server platform planning. This includes assessing the potential long-term impact on data center memory capacity and power efficiency, particularly for AI workloads, as the technology moves towards its anticipated volume production in the second half of 2027.

stories.title: Huawei Cloud launches latest AICS and expands enterprise AI agents
stories.summary: Huawei Cloud used the second day of HUAWEI CONNECT 2026 to launch an upgraded AI Cluster Service (AICS) and broaden its enterprise AI agent platform, announcements led by board director and CEO Peter Zhou. The moves target corporate customers building large-scale AI deployments.
stories.why_it_matters: Huawei is packaging cluster-scale compute with ready-made enterprise agents, competing directly with global cloud providers for corporate AI budgets. Customers in markets where Huawei operates face a viable alternative stack, intensifying pressure on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud in APAC and beyond.
stories.content:
- **Huawei Cloud launched its latest AICS.**
- **Huawei expanded its enterprise AI agent platform.**

Huawei Cloud has introduced a new version of its AI Cluster Service (AICS) and expanded its enterprise agent platform as part of announcements made during the second day of HUAWEI CONNECT 2026.

Peter Zhou, director of the board at Huawei and CEO of Huawei Cloud, announced the services during his keynote. The announcements also covered context memory storage, model services, two new areas within Huawei’s Industry AI Foundry, and plans to make AgentArts available outside China.

### AICS expands Huawei’s AI infrastructure

The latest AICS is designed for large-scale AI training and inference workloads. Huawei said the service uses a five-level recovery mechanism and full-chain observability to identify and respond to infrastructure faults.

According to Huawei, AICS has supported model training runs lasting more than 40 days and can recover from faults within 10 minutes. The company also said optimisations across scheduling, caching, and algorithms deliver 20% higher token throughput than the previous generation of the service.

Huawei did not provide independent benchmark results for the performance comparison.

Huawei first disclosed AICS in June, when it said the service uses its UnifiedBus interconnect and can support clusters containing more than 100,000 cards. UnifiedBus provides the high-bandwidth connections used to link computing resources across the cluster.

Huawei is increasingly connecting large numbers of processors into computing systems to compensate for limitations in individual chips. The approach forms part of the company’s broader Ascend AI computing roadmap.

AICS is scheduled to become commercially available in China on September 30, followed by markets outside China on November 30.

The international rollout comes as Huawei faces production constraints in its AI computing business. “Since we don’t have enough capacity to even satisfy the demand in China,” Huawei rotating chairman Eric Xu said, adding that the company does not plan a full-scale international expansion of its AI computing business for now.

Huawei also introduced Context Memory Storage, or CMS, for AI agents that need to retain and retrieve large volumes of contextual information during longer-running tasks. The company said CMS provides petabyte-scale storage and supports terabyte-scale memory reads.

Context memory systems can be used to store key-value, or KV, cache generated during model inference. KV cache retains previously computed information from a model’s context, reducing the amount of data that has to be recalculated as processing continues.

Separately, Huawei introduced its OceanStor M900 Context Memory Storage on the first day of HUAWEI CONNECT. The system extends KV cache from on-chip memory and DRAM to SSD storage, with Huawei saying UnifiedBus enables shared, tiered KV-cache storage of up to 64 PB in a single cluster.

Huawei claimed the CMS service offers twice the storage capacity and 50% higher performance than comparable products, although it did not disclose the products or benchmark methodology used for the comparison.

AICS and CMS sit within what Huawei calls Agentic Infra, which combines AI and general-purpose computing, storage, scheduling, and security capabilities for running AI agents. Huawei said Agentic Infra has served more than 3,500 customers.

### AgentArts and openJiuwen broaden the agent stack

Huawei is also expanding AgentArts, its platform for developing and managing enterprise AI agents.

The platform provides access to more than 5,000 general Model Context Protocol assets and more than 1,000 industry-specific MCP assets, according to Huawei. MCP provides a standardised way for AI applications and agents to connect with external data sources and tools.

Huawei said its enterprise agent platform has served more than 100 customers, including government organisations, utilities, research institutions, software companies, and healthcare organisations in China. AgentArts is scheduled to become commercially available in markets outside China on December 30.

Huawei is developing the platform alongside openJiuwen, its open-source agent framework.

Public openJiuwen repositories show that the framework includes Python and Java development kits, a distributed runtime, visual development tools, long-term memory components, and support for protocols including MCP and agent-to-agent communication. Its Apache 2.0-licensed core SDK supports workflow orchestration, tool calling, state management, debugging, and observability, while AI models are connected separately.

Huawei said the openJiuwen community has surpassed 50,000 stars and recorded 3.29 million downloads, although it did not specify how those figures were calculated.

Kingsoft Office demonstrated its use of Huawei Cloud’s agent platform at the event. The company has integrated the technology with WPS 365 Document Center and WPS Comate to develop office agents deployed in industries including finance and government.

Huawei also outlined its Agentic Model as a Service platform, which provides access to models from multiple providers without requiring customers to deploy the models themselves. MiniMax demonstrated its multimodal model with Huawei Cloud at the event, although Huawei did not disclose further commercial details for the MaaS service.

### Huawei extends industry and partner deployment programmes

Huawei Cloud has also expanded its Industry AI Foundry, a collection of industry-specific models, datasets, knowledge resources, agents, and implementation assets.

Huawei said the programme contains more than 1,000 industry assets and supports more than 1,000 deployed projects across healthcare, embodied AI, AI for science, manufacturing, and finance. The company did not provide a breakdown of the projects by deployment stage or scale.

Huawei added Smart Government and AI Hardware zones during the event.

The Smart Government Zone has 24 founding partners covering areas including government operations, public services, urban governance, and industry development. The AI Hardware Zone has 15 core partners and covers more than 20 device types, including AI glasses, AI toys, and AI recording cards.

Huawei said the AI Hardware Zone also includes more than 10 scenario templates and over 110 scenario skills.

Huawei separately introduced SCALE, a partner support programme covering solution development, testing, marketing, service delivery, and collaboration.

Leo Chen, Huawei senior vice president and president of Enterprise Sales, said the programme is intended to help partners take individual AI projects into wider deployments. “We want to help partners solve customer issues more efficiently and help customers achieve large-scale AI adoption,” Chen said.

Huawei is making reference architectures available for 48 scenarios, alongside testing and verification environments through its cloud-based OpenLab. The company said partners have used its products to develop more than 100 scenario-based solutions across eight industries.

Huawei is also providing access to its eFly and ePartner platforms for marketing, transactions, service operations, documentation, and technical tools. Its O3 Partner Service Enablement Platform provides partners with technical resources and service tools, while Huawei said its training and certification programmes have supported more than 50,000 AI professionals over the past three years.

stories.title: GreenSquare signs Sharon AI as first customer for SYD1 data centre campus
stories.summary: GreenSquareDC has signed Sharon AI as the anchor customer for the first stage of its SYD1 campus in Sydney, marking a concrete commitment for the development. The deal comes as Australia's AI data centre market shifts from announced projects toward signed tenants and construction.
stories.why_it_matters: Anchor pre-leasing is the industry's key de-risking step, converting pipeline announcements into financed builds. Sharon AI's commitment pressures competing Sydney campuses to secure their own tenants, and validates GreenSquare's positioning in the capital's tightening supply of AI-ready capacity.
stories.content:
Australian data centre developer and operator GreenSquare has signed a long-term contract with NASDAQ-listed Australian AI infrastructure provider Sharon AI, an NVIDIA Cloud Partner, for the first stage of its SYD1 data centre campus in Western Sydney. Sharon AI is expected to deploy approximately 8,200 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs at the site, with initial operations targeted for Q4 2026.

GreenSquare said the agreement anchors the first tranche of AI-ready capacity at SYD1, with initial operations targeted for the fourth quarter of 2026. The financial terms and contracted capacity associated with the agreement were not disclosed.

Sharon AI is a NVIDIA Cloud Partner and operates as an AI neocloud, providing infrastructure for organisations developing and deploying AI workloads. The company is expected to use the GreenSquare capacity for an NVIDIA HGX B300 deployment, which GreenSquare described as one of the largest publicly announced deployments of the platform in Australia.

The customer agreement provides a commercial milestone for GreenSquare as it develops a data centre portfolio across New South Wales and Victoria. The company said its broader development pipeline exceeds 1GW.

SYD1 is located in Norwest Business Park and is being developed as a 100MW-plus campus. Its first stage involves the adaptive reuse of an existing data centre building, rather than demolishing the structure and constructing a new facility.

GreenSquare said the reuse strategy has accelerated delivery while reducing embodied carbon compared with a conventional greenfield development. The company’s June sustainability assessment claimed the project retained 92 percent of the existing structural carbon, while achieving a 76 percent reduction in structural upfront carbon per square metre and a 93 percent reduction per kilowatt of IT capacity. The assessment was conducted independently by engineering consultancy TTW.

The existing building is being upgraded to support high-density computing, with GreenSquare highlighting power density and low water utilisation as design requirements. The company said the infrastructure is intended to accommodate changing customer requirements over time.

GreenSquare CEO Charles Penny said the customer commitment validated the company’s platform and demand for AI-ready infrastructure that can be delivered with speed and operational discipline. “Our focus now is on execution – bringing next-generation capacity online safely, reliably and on schedule,” he said.

In March, GreenSquare said the proposed 80MW SYD1 Stage 2 had been endorsed for support through the NSW Government’s Investment Delivery Authority (IDA). The programme provides practical, non-financial assistance, including coordination with government agencies and support in addressing infrastructure and regulatory issues.

stories.content:
Singapore: Digital Realty, a major global data centre operator, maintains command centres worldwide, including a key hub in Singapore, to provide 24/7 oversight of its more than 300 facilities across six continents. These centres are crucial for ensuring the uninterrupted operation of critical online services, including banking, messaging, and artificial intelligence (AI) functionalities.Analysts at the Singapore command centre monitor digital maps and dashboards, focusing on early detection of warning signs like sudden temperature increases to prevent disruptions. Daniel Naing, a team member, highlighted the importance of a steady nerve in handling thousands of system alerts weekly, emphasising the indispensable human element in data centre management despite increasing automation.Digital Realty leases server space to approximately 6,000 companies, facing common issues such as power disruptions and equipment failures. The company also implements detailed protocols for natural disasters like earthquakes and typhoons, maintaining readiness for potential threats.

The booming demand for data centres, particularly for AI, has raised public concerns about their environmental impact. Serene Nah, managing director and head of Asia Pacific at Digital Realty, noted that data centres are essential infrastructure, almost a matter of national security, requiring constant uptime. She stressed the importance of addressing public misconceptions about carbon emissions and water usage.To counter these concerns, Digital Realty prioritises renewable energy solutions such as solar panels and closed-loop server cooling systems that continuously recycle water. stories.title: AI fuels M&A deals across Australia and Southeast Asia
stories.summary: AI is fuelling dealmaking across Australia and Southeast Asia, with buyers chasing proprietary tech, scalable models and data centre capacity.
stories.content:
Mon, 21st Sep 2026 (Yesterday)
### Key Insights

- AI continues to drive M&A activity across Australia and Southeast Asia
- Investors are prioritising proprietary technology, AI capability and scalable business models
- Growing demand for AI infrastructure is creating new investment opportunities, particularly in data centres and digital infrastructure.

Artiﬁcial intelligence (AI) continued to be a key driver of M&A activity in 2026. Across the region, we are seeing increased investment activity and transactions where digital transformation and AI capability are becoming prerequisites for investment decisions. We expect this trend to continue as investors increasingly seek businesses with proprietary technologies in AI and skill sets that can drive the technology.

### Investor-friendly markets continue to attract AI investment

Southeast Asia, particularly in Singapore and Indonesia, appears to remain attractive for private equity and venture capital activity. The VC ecosystems and emerging technologies continue to grow, as do the deals supporting investment in the sector. With increasing adoption and development of AI across businesses, investors are ﬁnding an abundance of acquisition targets in high-growth markets across the region that can be selected and scaled for growth.

Technology-driven growth in markets such as Singapore and Australia also remains a key theme in cross-border transactions. The ease of doing business, strong growth prospects and productivity gains from AI transformation continue to make these investor-friendly countries attractive targets.

While Southeast Asia is a focal point for growth in the technology and AI sectors, the Australian M&A market appears to be focused on acquiring niche AI businesses rather than developing growth stories. Australia's robust and stable regulatory regime and mature technology sector are signiﬁcant drawcards for investors, particularly when combined with a growing VC ecosystem across the country's major cities. Even smaller markets such as Canberra are experiencing signiﬁcant investments and cross-border deal activity in this space.

### AI Infrastructure

The rapid growth of AI is also driving increased investment in support infrastructure. Demand for hyperscale data centres continues to increase as businesses invest in the computing power and storage capacity required to support the use of AI.

Melbourne appears to be the fastest growing centre for data centre investment due to the abundance of land opportunities compared to Sydney. How the regulatory landscape evolves alongside the adoption of AI infrastructure and related M&A activity will be an interesting trend to watch.

### Looking ahead

M&A activity involving AI is expected to remain strong across the region over the next 12 months. As investors become increasingly selective on deals with AI fuelled companies, businesses with strong ﬁnancials and a defendable pipeline of potential business will continue to attract interest, particularly as AI adoption expands across industries.

The Australian Prime Minister's recent announcement of an AI Ofﬁce only heightens the prominence of AI in the M&A landscape in Australia and the Southeast Asia.
